title: Amazon.com, the online bookstore, goes public
what: Amazon.com of Seattle sold 3 million shares on the Nasdaq on May 15 at $18 each. The company, which opened as 'Earth's Biggest Bookstore' on the World Wide Web in July 1995, had sales of $15.7 million in 1996, up from $511,000, and a net loss of $5.8 million. Founder Jeff Bezos says it will keep spending to grow; Barnes & Noble sued it days before the listing over its claim to be the world's largest bookstore.
why: The listing beat (importance 1). The case for buying: the fastest-growing shop on the young internet with a famous brand; the case against: no profit in sight. A share at the IPO was worth over 3,000 times as much by 2026.

title: Amazon's sales jump twelvefold
what: Amazon's sales in the quarter to June were $27.9 million, against $2.2 million a year earlier, as more customers bought and existing customers came back. The company is still losing money, spending heavily on marketing.
why: The first quarter reported as a public company confirms the growth; the shares rose 55% in July. The figures are from the quarterly filing; the exact date of the earnings release was not confirmed.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1018724/0000891020-97-001148.txt (10-Q for the quarter to June 30, 1997, read 2026-10-03)

title: Amazon borrows $75 million
what: Amazon arranged a $75 million three-year secured loan with Deutsche Bank on November 7 to finance its growth, on top of the money raised in its May listing.
why: Small in hindsight, but a sign of how much cash the build-out needed; Bezos cited the IPO and this loan as giving Amazon 'substantial strategic flexibility'.

title: Amazon buys bookstores in Britain and Germany, splits its shares
what: On April 27 Amazon reported sales of $87.4 million for the first quarter, up 446% from a year earlier, and a net loss of $9.3 million. It has more than 2.26 million customer accounts. It announced a two-for-one share split and the purchase of online booksellers in the UK and Germany and of the Internet Movie Database.
why: The first step abroad and beyond books.

title: Amazon's holiday sales quadruple
what: On January 26 Amazon reported fourth-quarter sales of $252.9 million, up 283%, and sales of $610 million for 1998, up 313%. It has more than 6.2 million customers and leads in books, music and video online. The net loss for the quarter was $46.4 million; the finance chief warned that low prices and fast growth keep margins thin.
why: Growth at any price, rewarded by the market: the shares rose another 1,108% in the twelve months to March 1999.

title: Amazon backs Pets.com
what: Amazon led a $10.5 million investment in Pets.com, a San Francisco start-up that sells pet food and supplies online, taking a majority stake. Amazon is investing in a string of young online shops.
why: Amazon's investments in dot-com start-ups later cost it hundreds of millions in write-offs; Pets.com closed in November 2000.

title: Amazon grows 84% but keeps losing money
what: On July 26 Amazon reported second-quarter sales of $578 million, up 84%, a pro forma operating loss of $89 million and $908 million of cash. The day before, it announced the resignation of its president. Investors have turned against loss-making internet companies.
why: The shares were down about 65% from their 1999 high by July 2000 (-17% in the month).

title: Amazon cuts 1,300 jobs
what: On January 30 Amazon reported fourth-quarter sales of $972 million, up 44%, and 2000 sales of $2.76 billion. The quarter's net loss was $545 million, including $339 million of write-downs on goodwill and investments in other internet companies. It is cutting about 1,300 jobs, 15% of its workforce, closing a distribution centre in Georgia and running its Seattle centre only in season.
why: The darkest stretch: the shares fell 93% from March 1999 to September 2001.

title: Amazon's losses narrow
what: Amazon reported first-quarter sales of $700 million, up 22% from a year earlier. Technology shares rallied in April after months of falls.
why: The first hint that Amazon could survive the crash; the shares rose 54% in the month. The release date in late April was not confirmed (the quarterly filing is dated April 27).
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1018724/000095010901500823/d10q.htm (10-Q for the quarter to March 31, 2001, read 2026-10-03)

title: Amazon makes its first profit
what: Amazon reported a net profit of $5 million for the fourth quarter of 2001, its first, on sales of more than $1 billion. For the full year it still lost $567 million on sales of $3.12 billion. The company warned that the quarterly profit should not be taken as a trend.
why: The turning point for the doubters; the shares rose 31% in January.

title: Amazon's first profitable year
what: Amazon reported net income of $35 million for 2003, its first profitable year, against a loss of $149 million in 2002. Fourth-quarter net income was $73 million.
why: The business model is proven; the shares had risen almost ninefold from their 2001 low by the end of 2003.

title: Amazon's sales grow 26%
what: On July 26 Amazon reported second-quarter sales of $1.75 billion, up 26%, and net income of $52 million, down from $76 million a year earlier. Operating income excluding currency effects grew 27%.
why: Steady growth after a weak first half; the shares rose 36% in July.

title: Amazon's profit falls as it spends on technology
what: Amazon reported second-quarter sales of $2.14 billion, up 22%, but net income fell to $22 million from $52 million a year earlier. The company keeps spending on technology, and new businesses such as web services for other companies.
why: Investors balk at Bezos's spending; the shares fell 30% in July 2006, the low before the long rise.

title: Amazon's profit more than doubles
what: On April 24 Amazon reported first-quarter sales of $3.02 billion, up 32%, and net income of $111 million, up 115%. Operating income rose 38%.
why: Proof that the spending pays; the shares rose 54% in April, and the profile shifts to the low-price, many-sellers flywheel.

title: Amazon keeps growing in the crisis
what: On October 22 Amazon reported third-quarter sales of $4.26 billion, up 31%, and net income of $118 million, up 48%. Its Kindle electronic reader now offers 185,000 books, and Kindle titles make up more than 10% of unit sales of books available in both forms.
why: Amazon fell with the market (-21% in October, -25% in November 2008) despite growing, then recovered fast.

title: Kindle becomes Amazon's best-seller
what: On October 22 Amazon reported third-quarter sales of $5.45 billion, up 28%, and net income of $199 million, up 68%. The Kindle reader is now the best-selling item on Amazon.com, and a new model with international wireless costs $259.
why: A strong quarter in the recession; the shares rose 27% in October 2009 and doubled during the year.

title: Amazon sells the Kindle Fire at $199 and profits drop
what: On October 25 Amazon reported third-quarter sales of $10.88 billion, up 44%, but net income fell 73% to $63 million. It is launching the Kindle Fire tablet at $199 and other Kindles from $79.
why: Bezos sacrifices profit for growth once more; the market tolerated it after a short dip (-10% in November and December 2011).

title: Amazon grows 24% while barely breaking even
what: On October 24 Amazon reported third-quarter sales of $17.09 billion, up 24%, and a net loss of $41 million. It is hiring 70,000 seasonal warehouse workers for the holidays and making its own television pilots.
why: The classic Amazon quarter of the 2010s: growth, investment, no profit, rising shares (+16% in October 2013).

title: Amazon reveals its cloud is a $5 billion business
what: For the first time Amazon reported Amazon Web Services, which rents computing power and storage to other companies, as a separate segment. Bezos called it 'a $5 billion business and still growing fast'. First-quarter sales rose 15% to $22.7 billion, with a small net loss.
why: Investors discover that the cloud, not the shop, is Amazon's profit engine; the shares rose 13% in April and much more in the months after.

title: Amazon surprises with a profit
what: Amazon reported second-quarter net income of $92 million against a loss a year earlier, on sales up 20% to $23.2 billion. Operating income was $464 million.
why: The shares rose 24% in July 2015, the start of a decade in which Amazon became one of the most valuable companies in the world.

title: Amazon buys Whole Foods
what: Amazon agreed to buy Whole Foods Market, an upmarket supermarket chain with more than 400 stores, for about $13.7 billion. It is Amazon's first big step into physical shops.
why: Amazon's largest acquisition and its move into everyday shopping.

title: Amazon's sales jump 38% in the holiday quarter
what: Amazon reported fourth-quarter sales of $60.5 billion, up 38%, and net income of $1.9 billion. Sales for 2017 rose 31% to $177.9 billion.
why: Growth of this size is rare; the shares rose 24% in January 2018 ahead of the report.

title: Amazon drops its New York headquarters plan
what: On February 14 Amazon said it will not build its planned second headquarters in Queens, New York, after local opposition, and will concentrate on Arlington, Virginia, where it plans at least 25,000 jobs.
why: A rare public retreat for Amazon, a sign of the political resistance it faces.

title: The pandemic sends shoppers to Amazon
what: With shops closed by the Covid-19 pandemic, Amazon is hiring about 175,000 extra warehouse and delivery workers. On April 30 it reported first-quarter sales of $75.5 billion, up 26%; net income fell to $2.5 billion from $3.6 billion.
why: The pandemic winner: the shares rose 27% in April 2020 and about three quarters over the year.

title: Bezos hands over to Andy Jassy
what: On February 2 Amazon announced that founder Jeff Bezos will become executive chair in the third quarter and that Andy Jassy, head of Amazon Web Services, will become chief executive. Sales in 2020 rose 38% to $386 billion and fourth-quarter net income more than doubled to $7.2 billion.
why: The founder steps back at the peak of the pandemic boom.

title: Amazon reports a loss as growth stalls
what: On April 28 Amazon reported a first-quarter net loss of $3.8 billion, against a profit of $8.1 billion a year earlier, as sales grew only 7% to $116.4 billion and operating income fell to $3.7 billion. The pandemic surge in online shopping has faded and costs have risen.
why: The shares fell 24% in April and ended 2022 about half their 2021 high; layoffs of 18,000 and then 27,000 followed.

title: Amazon's sales beat expectations despite a loss
what: Amazon reported second-quarter sales of $121.2 billion, up 7%, and a net loss of $2.0 billion, against a profit of $7.8 billion a year earlier. Its shares were split twenty-for-one on May 27.
why: Relief after a terrible first half; the shares rose 27% in July 2022, before falling to new lows in December.

title: Amazon invests in the AI start-up Anthropic
what: Amazon will invest up to $4 billion in Anthropic, an artificial intelligence start-up, starting with $1.25 billion. Anthropic will use Amazon Web Services as its main cloud and make its models available to AWS customers.
why: Amazon's main bet on generative AI; it invested further in 2024 and 2026.

title: Amazon's profit soars
what: Amazon reported fourth-quarter net income of $10.6 billion, against $0.3 billion a year earlier, on sales of $170.0 billion, up 14%. AWS sales grew 13% to $24.2 billion. Sales for 2023 were $574.8 billion.
why: Cost cuts after the 2022-23 layoffs pay off; +14% in February 2024.

title: Amazon earns $20 billion in a quarter
what: Amazon reported fourth-quarter net income of $20.0 billion on sales of $187.8 billion, up 10%. AWS sales grew 19% to $28.8 billion. Sales for 2024 were $638.0 billion.
why: Record profits; the shares nonetheless fell 11% in February and 10% in March 2025.

title: Amazon's cloud accelerates
what: On April 29 Amazon reported first-quarter sales of $181.5 billion, up 17%, with AWS sales up 28% to $37.6 billion and net income of $30.3 billion. Earlier in the month Amazon invested a further $5 billion in Anthropic.
why: AI demand for cloud computing lifts the shares 27% in April 2026, in a strong month for the market (+10%).
